validator: draft 1 passes validate.mjs with no problems, soft problems or warnings.
keep: The idea is named up front in two plain sentences (times −1 is a half turn, so the quarter turn done twice does its job, and that quarter turn is j with j × j = −1), and the bold recap says it back with [1], [2] and [3] on the words their quotes support.

The picture shows the cause the brief asks for: × −1 drawn as a turn, a turn handle that finds the turn which done twice makes the half turn, and × j stepping 1, j, −1, −j, 1, so j × j = −1 is watched happening (brief, lesson 1).
Thirteen screens alternate SHOW and DO, ending on mixed puzzles (j⁵, x² + 4 = 0), each with three answers whose wrong ones are named slips.

Every lesson-1 misconception in the brief has a puzzle with its own hint: × −1 as a mirror (the turn-twice puzzle, step 4), the sign of a power of j (j³ with j and −1 offered, step 6), √ of a negative (j3 × j2 with 6 offered, step 10). 'Imaginary' is named once and set aside in ignores.

The √−1 question is shown both ways, as the brief decided: mathcentre's j = √−1 then j² = −1 [3], and this course's j × j = −1 first, with its reason computed on screen (√36 = 6 against j2 × j3 = −6).
The quadratic from Quadratics is finished with numbers computed from the formula, and the practice example is checked by substituting back.
Why j and not i is cited [4]; the analogy is the phasor from Trigonometry, with where it breaks.
fix: False 'only' (the central one): 'Its turn done twice must make 180°, so it is 90°.' Three quarter turns, 270°, done twice is 540°, a half turn and a full turn, and also lands on −1. That is −j. Say both: the quarter turn anticlockwise is j, the quarter turn clockwise (three quarter turns anticlockwise) is −j, and the handle shows both. This also gives the two answers to x² = −9 their cause.
False absolute: '√a × √b = √(ab) breaks for negatives.' It holds when only one is negative (√−4 × √9 = j2 × 3 = j6 = √−36). Say it breaks when both are negative.

False absolute in practice: 'only a turn has a half' is stated loosely. Say it as the picture shows it: a turn can be split into two equal turns, and a flip cannot be split into two equal moves that each leave the arrow the same length.
Unsourced fact not flagged: 'Maths books write i for the same number.' Fold it into the [4] sentence, whose quote says engineers use j instead of i.
Qualifier widened: 'Many books, mathcentre among them' has no source for 'many'. Say 'Some books, mathcentre among them'.

Plan detail stated as fact about an earlier course: 'in Quadratics x² + 2x + 5 = 0 had no real roots'. Quadratics taught 'no real roots' for a negative b² − 4ac; this equation is this lesson's example. Say it that way.
Talks about the idea: 'Here is why a new number is needed' and 'That gives the powers of j from the rule, with no new facts' announce instead of teach. Cut them.
The numbers list has no step 2 entry for its puzzle (which number squares to −9). Add the slip −3 × −3 = 9 and the turn handle's 270° and 540°.
